titulo: Teaching adults: the 5 principles that make the class use it on Monday
lead: Adults don't learn AI by sitting through a lecture. They learn when they see the why, work on a problem of their own, practice with feedback, try to remember without looking, and use it again the following week. This lesson turns that into 5 principles and a lesson plan you can reuse in every workshop.
objetivo: plan an AI lesson for adults with the 5 principles marked: why, real problem, practice, retrieval, and next week.

aprende.t: The 5 principles and where each one comes from
Why an AI lecture doesn't change anyone's work
How to swap a generic example for the learner's own task

hero_alt: Adults at a work table doing a hands-on exercise on laptops, one showing the screen to a colleague.

secoes.sub: Each block is a moment in your lesson. Click to see what to do.

nos.detalhe: Adults ask "what is this for in my work?" before they pay attention. Open with the problem the class already feels (a queue of messages, a report that eats the afternoon) and only then show the tool. It comes from Malcolm Knowles' theory of adult learning: the need to know.

The exercise uses the task the person does every week, not a textbook example. Juliana, in customer service, practices with a customer complaint; Patrícia, in sales, with a proposal. The learner's experience is the material of the lesson.

Deliberate practice: a task a little above what the person already does, with immediate feedback and a second attempt. Showing 10 features is worth less than doing 1 task twice, with the second better than the first.

Ask before you re-explain. Trying to remember (even getting it wrong) fixes more than rereading: it's the testing effect, measured in labs and in classrooms. A 3-question quiz at the end is worth more than a summary read aloud.

nos.sub: space it out and apply it
nos.detalhe: What isn't used within 7 days disappears. End with a commitment (1 real task during the week) and come back to the topic a few days later, with a short exercise. Spacing the review pays off more than cramming everything into one day.

secoes.legenda: Why and real problem hold attention; practice, retrieval, and next week make the habit stick.
secoes.dica: If you only have time for one principle, keep the real problem: it's what changes the outcome of an AI workshop the most.

secoes.sub: What changes in how you teach. Click each tab.

texto: Start with the cost of the problem, with a number from the company itself: "how many messages go unanswered after 6 p.m.?".
Name the fear early ("will this replace me?") and calmly say what the lesson changes and what it doesn't.

exemplo.texto: Today you're going to leave able to answer complaints in half the time, without losing control of what goes to the customer.

texto: Ask before the lesson: "bring a text, spreadsheet, or message you used this week" (no customer personal data).
Without learner material, use the lab company, with the industry vocabulary: order, route, invoice, exchange.

exemplo.texto: Instead of "write a poem about AI", use "summarize yesterday's 5 complaints and say which one needs action today".

texto: Round 1: the person does it alone. You walk around and don't touch anyone's mouse. Round 2: they redo it with the feedback they received.
Before each new block, ask what stuck from the previous one. Wait 15 seconds for an answer.

exemplo.texto: Without looking at the slide: what are the 3 things you check before sending the reply to the customer?

texto: Each person writes down 1 task they will do with AI in the next 7 days and who they will show the result to.
Schedule a short follow-up (15 minutes, a few days later) with 2 retrieval questions and the cases from the week.

exemplo.texto: By Friday, I'll use the reply template on 10 complaints and show 2 of them to Juliana.

secoes.sub: The lesson plan is your mold for every lesson in this program.

blocos.conteudo:
LESSON PLAN · <topic> · <class> · <duration>
Objective (verb + what the person can do afterward):
<...>

[1] WHY (up to 5 min)
- Problem the class already feels: <...>
- Company number that shows the cost: <...>
- Fear to name: <...>

[2] REAL PROBLEM
- Learner material requested beforehand: <...>
- Backup (lab company): <...>

[3] PRACTICE (round 1 and round 2)
- Task: <...>
- How the person knows they got it right: <...>
- Feedback I give between rounds: <...>

[4] RETRIEVAL
- 3 questions without looking at the material: <...> / <...> / <...>

[5] NEXT WEEK
- Each person's commitment: 1 task in 7 days
- Follow-up scheduled: <date> · 15 min

FINAL CHECK
[ ] the 5 principles appear above
[ ] more practice time than talking time
[ ] no real personal customer data in the exercise

blocos.rot: Prompt · adapt the exercise to the class
blocos.conteudo:
I'm going to teach an AI lesson to <area and roles> at a <type and size of company>.
Tasks they do every week: <list 3 to 5>.

Create 3 hands-on 10-minute exercises, one per task, with:
1. the request the learner makes to the AI (with expected result and format);
2. what they should check in the response before using it;
3. how they know they got it right (done when).
Use the real vocabulary of the area. Do not use real personal data.
Don't invent company numbers: leave <number> where I should fill them in.

secoes.sub: Do it with a lesson you will actually teach.

exercicios.texto: Copy the lesson plan and fill it in for a 30- to 60-minute lesson about one use of AI at work for a class you know (or for the customer service team at Horizonte Distribuidora).
exercicios.pronto: the plan is saved and each of the 5 principles has one line filled in and checked; practice takes up more time than explanation.

exercicios.texto: Take a generic example you usually use ("ask for a poem", "ask for the capital of France") and swap it for a real task from the class's area, using the adaptation prompt.
exercicios.pronto: you have 1 new exercise with a request, what to check, and a "done when" the person can verify on their own.

secoes.sub: 4 questions. The explanation appears after your attempt.

perguntas.p: The class is distracted in the first few minutes. Which principle was missing?
opcoes: Why: the class didn't see their own problem before the tool
perguntas.explica: Adults pay attention when they see what something is for. Opening with the tool ("today we'll look at feature X") is the common mistake; open with the cost of the problem, using a company number.

perguntas.p: You have 60 minutes. Which split follows the principles?
opcoes: 45 min of demonstration and 15 of questions
15 min of context and 45 of practice in two rounds, with retrieval in the middle
perguntas.explica: Deliberate practice means doing, getting feedback, and redoing. A long demonstration gives the feeling of learning, but nobody leaves able to do it.

perguntas.p: At the end of the lesson, what best locks in the content?
opcoes: Three questions answered without looking at the material
perguntas.explica: Trying to remember, even when you get it wrong, locks in more than rereading (the testing effect). The PDF helps later, but it doesn't replace retrieval.

perguntas.p: Why ask learners for a piece of their own work material before the lesson?
opcoes: Because the learner's real problem is what keeps the use going after the lesson
perguntas.explica: Practice on the real task becomes habit; a textbook example stays in the classroom. Careful: ask for material without customer personal data.

itens.texto: Open with the cost the class feels, and use their own task in the exercise.
Doing, getting feedback and redoing is worth more than seeing ten features.
Ask before re-explaining; short quiz at the end.
Commitment to 1 task and a follow-up scheduled a few days later.
